justification: Round 1 capped this article at 7.0 for exactly one reason: the :::dotnet callout claimed the O(n)-on-reallocation exception was unique to Stack<T>.Push, implying Queue<T>.Enqueue was pure O(1), and linked only the Queue<T> class-overview page (which carries no Big-O language at all) instead of the method pages. That is fixed. I fetched all four Microsoft Learn method pages directly in this round: Queue<T>.Enqueue's Remarks read 'If Count is less than the capacity of the internal array, this method is an O(1) operation. If the internal array needs to be reallocated to accommodate the new element, this method becomes an O(n) operation' -- word-for-word the same shape of exception Stack<T>.Push documents ('If Count is less than the capacity of the stack, Push is an O(1) operation. If the capacity needs to be increased ... Push becomes an O(n) operation'). Queue<T>.Dequeue's Remarks are just 'This method is an O(1) operation,' with no reallocation exception, and Stack<T>.Pop's Remarks are the same: 'This method is an O(1) operation.' The rewritten callout states this exactly: Enqueue and Push are each O(1) except on the one call that forces a reallocation, which both document as O(n); Dequeue and Pop are plain O(1) with no such exception. All four method pages are now hyperlinked inline and listed in front-matter sources with today's access date. The 'Queue<T> is documented as a circular array' claim is also independently confirmed on the class page: 'This class implements a generic queue as a circular array... As elements are added to a Queue<T>, the capacity is automatically increased as required by reallocating the internal array.' I re-ran the 'What both cost' program myself outside the article's own harness (a standalone dotnet run of the exact BuildLayered/CountBfsEdges/CountDfsEdges code, copied verbatim) and got the identical table the article prints: layers 2/4/6/8 -> verts 6/15/28/45, edges 8/40/112/240, BFS 8/40/112/240, DFS 8/40/112/240 -- confirming the regenerated, mobile-shortened headers and narrower column widths did not silently change any digit.
